import math
print('Tier-boundary update check (all initial weights equal):')
for t in [3,4,5]:
    n=2**(2**t)
    eps=1e-6
    w=(1-eps)/n
    wp=(1+eps)/n
    old=math.floor(math.log2(math.log2(1/w)))
    new=math.floor(math.log2(math.log2(1/wp)))
    expected_rot=math.log(n)+0.5772156649015329+1/(2*n)-1
    print({'n':n,'old_tier':old,'new_tier':new,'log2_weight_ratio':math.log2(wp/w),'expected_rotations_for_extreme_key_approx':expected_rot})
print('Negative-tier chain in stated B-tree construction:')
for k in [3,5,8]:
    log2_B=2**k
    tiers=[math.floor(math.log2(2**j/log2_B)) for j in range(k+1)]
    print({'log2_B':log2_B,'heavy_key_tiers':tiers,'target_logB_inverse_weight':1,'separate_tier_blocks_on_path':len(tiers)})
print('Nearly concentrated static distribution:')
m=1000000

strengths: The composite priority rule is simple, and the tier-by-tier ancestor analysis provides a clear route to a distribution-independent O(1 + log(1/w_x)) expected-depth bound. The counterexamples to direct-frequency and single-logarithm priorities help explain the design.

The static cross-entropy upper bound offers an interpretable connection between prediction error and access cost. The working-set score is also an interesting construction for representing temporal locality through locally changing weights.
The empirical study includes several classical and learning-augmented baselines, ten independent trials, and controlled prediction perturbations, providing a useful starting point for evaluation.
weaknesses: The weight-update guarantee in Corollary 2.7 is false for the stated priority rule. Let n = 2^(2^t) and place every weight just below 1/n, giving a standard random treap. Raising one weight just above 1/n moves that item into a higher-priority tier and forces it to the root. This requires Θ(log n) expected rotations although |log(w'/w)| can be arbitrarily small. The analogous guarantee in Theorem 3.1 is also unsupported: deleting and reinserting establishes a sum of access costs, not their logarithmic difference. These are substantive issues for the subsequent dynamic analyses.

The B-tree construction in Appendix C does not establish its claimed depth bound. It sums only nonnegative tiers, although negative tiers need not contain only constantly many items when B grows. For example, with B = 2^(2^k), ordered weights w_j = 2^(-2^j), j = 0,...,k, occupy distinct tiers j-k. The stated construction puts these singleton components in separate blocks, giving the item of weight 1/B depth k+1 instead of O(1). Padding with sufficiently light keys can satisfy the stated n-versus-B conditions. The high-probability proof additionally assumes B = O(sqrt(C_t)) without establishing it for individual tiers.

Several robustness claims exceed what the proofs establish. Theorem 2.13 gives an upper bound involving cross-entropy, not an exact increase of m times KL divergence as claimed in the overview. Theorem D.2 similarly substitutes the actual ideal-prediction cost for an upper-bound expression, which does not justify Theorem 4.5's additive comparison. Moreover, Corollary C.6 incorrectly uses a lower bound on p_x as a lower bound on the predicted probability q_x. Additive closeness permits arbitrarily small q_x; without a specified smoothing rule, this proof and the dependent C.7–C.9 guarantees are unsupported.

The experimental results contain unexplained inconsistencies that undermine the superiority claims. Under the stated exactly uniform predictions, all proposed priorities have the same tier, so the proposed and standard random treaps are identically distributed. Figure 4 nevertheless reports a large systematic advantage. Figure 5 also shows prediction-free baselines changing substantially with KL divergence, without clearly explaining whether the access workload changes. Resolving these observations requires a precise generation protocol, consistent comparison accounting, and auditable implementation details.

The contribution needs clearer positioning against classical weighted randomized search trees. Weighted treaps using independent exponential priorities with rates proportional to item weights already yield O(1 + log(W/w_x)) expected depth. The manuscript discusses ordinary treaps and Lin et al. but does not explain the benefit of its construction relative to this weighted alternative. The proposed combination should also be distinguished from established prediction-free working-set structures.

The dynamic results assume access to future distinct-item working-set information; the suggested causal proxies are neither analyzed nor evaluated. Experiments cover static synthetic comparison counts, without evaluating dynamic maintenance costs or the proposed B-tree's I/O behavior. Consequently, they provide limited support for the broader practical claims about dynamic and external-memory performance.

A repairable but pervasive theorem-statement issue is the missing additive constant in access bounds. Depth explicitly counts vertices, so it is at least one. For two keys with frequencies m-1 and 1, mH(p) is only Θ(log m), while processing the sequence requires at least m comparisons. The static bounds therefore need O(m(1 + H(p))) and corresponding corrections elsewhere. Presentation also needs correction: Section 5.1 inconsistently describes the varying quantity, and Figure 7's caption reverses working-set and interval-set properties.
